questions.stem: With reference to hydrogen bonding and dispersion forces, explain the trends in the boiling point data of these compounds, within each series and between the series.
questions.stimulus:
The boiling points for two series of compounds are listed.
[Figure: Two tables of boiling points (°C): amines methanamine −6, ethanamine 17, propan-1-amine 48, butan-1-amine 78; alcohols methanol 65, ethanol 78, propan-1-ol 97, butan-1-ol 118.]

criteria.text: Explains increase in boiling point with increasing carbon number due to increasing dispersion forces; Explains difference in boiling point between series with reference to difference in strength of hydrogen bonding
Explains ONE trend OR Describes trends
Makes a relevant comparison to a data series
Provides some relevant information

questions.sampleAnswer: For both the alcohols and the amines, dispersion forces will increase with increasing carbon number, due to increased number of electrons present, leading to increased boiling points. However, for any given carbon number, the alcohol has stronger hydrogen bonding than the corresponding amine, as oxygen has a higher electronegativity than nitrogen, so the alcohols all have higher boiling points than the corresponding amines.

figure.alt: Two tables of boiling points (°C): amines methanamine −6, ethanamine 17, propan-1-amine 48, butan-1-amine 78; alcohols methanol 65, ethanol 78, propan-1-ol 97, butan-1-ol 118.

questions.stem: Using collision theory, explain the rate of reaction between t = 0 min and t = 6 min. Refer to the [I₂] in your answer.
questions.stimulus: At t = 0 min, I₂ was added to a mixture of HCN, I⁻ and H⁺, bringing [I₂] to 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹. After 3 minutes, the system was at equilibrium, and an analysis of the mixture found that half of the I₂ had reacted.

criteria.text: Provides an explanation of the rate of reaction with clear link to [I₂] and collision theory
Provides some description of the rate of reaction with link to [I₂] and/or collision theory
Provides some relevant information

questions.sampleAnswer: The initial high [I₂] results in more frequent successful collisions and a high rate of forward reaction. As the reaction proceeds, I₂ is consumed, so [I₂] decreases, so the reaction rate decreases. After t = 3 min, the system is at equilibrium so the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are the same, so [I₂] is constant.

questions.stem: Which of these two processes is preferable for urea production? Justify your answer with reference to the information provided.
questions.stimulus:
The atom economy (AE) of a reaction is a measure of the mass of atoms in the starting materials that are incorporated into the desired product. Higher AE means lower mass of waste products. Urea can be produced in a variety of ways. One way is to react ammonia (high toxicity) with phosgene (high toxicity). Another way is to react ammonia with dimethyl carbonate (DMC, low toxicity). The chemical equations and AE for these two processes are provided.
[Figure: Two reactions to urea: phosgene with 4NH₃ giving urea and 2NH₄Cl (AE 35.9%); dimethyl carbonate with 2NH₃ giving urea and 2CH₃OH (AE 48.4%).]

criteria.text: Correctly compares the processes and justifies preferred approach
Compares one aspect of the processes
Provides some relevant information

questions.sampleAnswer: The atom economy for the reaction with DMC is 48.4% compared to the phosgene reaction at 35.9%. As a result, there is less waste in the process involving the less harmful DMC. Less ammonia is also required (2 moles, in place of 4 for phosgene). This comparison identifies the production of urea from DMC as the preferred approach in terms of atom economy, toxicity of starting materials and quantities of harmful reactants required.

figure.alt: Two reactions to urea: phosgene with 4NH₃ giving urea and 2NH₄Cl (AE 35.9%); dimethyl carbonate with 2NH₃ giving urea and 2CH₃OH (AE 48.4%).

questions.stem: Explain how ¹³C NMR spectroscopy could be used to monitor the progress of this reaction.
questions.stimulus:
Acetone can be reduced, as shown.
[Figure: Reduction of acetone (a ketone, C=O) to propan-2-ol (an alcohol, CH–OH), drawn as skeletal structures.]

criteria.text: Provides a sound explanation of how key ¹³C NMR spectral features can be used to monitor the reaction
Provides some explanation of how key ¹³C NMR spectral features can be used to monitor the reaction
Provides some relevant information

questions.sampleAnswer: In the ¹³C NMR spectrum of the reaction mixture at the start of the reaction, there will be two (2) signals, due to the 2 different carbons (C=O and CH₃) in the reactant molecule. However, as the reaction proceeds, the C=O bond is transformed to H—C—OH. Therefore, a new signal will appear in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of the reaction mixture that corresponds to the different carbon environment in the product. This peak will appear as the reaction proceeds, while the original peak for C=O will disappear.

figure.alt: Reduction of acetone (a ketone, C=O) to propan-2-ol (an alcohol, CH–OH), drawn as skeletal structures.

questions.stem: Explain the shape of the graph. Include TWO balanced chemical equations in your answer.
questions.stimulus:
An aqueous solution of ammonia is added to a solution containing hydrochloric acid. A plot of conductivity against volume of ammonia solution added is shown. The temperature of the solution is kept constant throughout and the conductivity of the solution is corrected for dilution. The relative conductivities of some relevant ions are shown in the table.
[Figure: Line graph of conductivity against volume of ammonia added (0 to 10 mL), with a minimum near 4.5 mL, and a table of relative conductivities of H⁺, OH⁻, Cl⁻ and NH₄⁺.]

criteria.text: Provides a thorough explanation of the shape of the graph ; Includes TWO balanced chemical equations
Provides a sound explanation of the shape of the graph ; Includes a balanced chemical equation
Demonstrates some understanding of the shape of the graph
Provides some relevant information

figure.alt: Line graph of conductivity against volume of ammonia added (0 to 10 mL), with a minimum near 4.5 mL, and a table of relative conductivities of H⁺, OH⁻, Cl⁻ and NH₄⁺.

questions.sampleAnswerTruncated: Before the equivalence point (below 4.5 mL), hydrochloric acid is being neutralised by the added ammonia: This has the effect of replacing H⁺ ions (high conductivity) with NH₄⁺ ions (low conductivity), so the conductivity decreases. After the equivalence point, the excess ammonia added will produce some NH₄⁺ and OH⁻ ions, both of which have greater conductivity than the reactant molecules: This reaction only occurs to a small extent, however, as the NH₄⁺ already present in the solution will suppress this ionisation, in accordance with Le Châtelier’s Principle. Accordingly, the conductivity only increases slightly after the equivalence point.

questions.stem: Explain, with reference to the information provided, why this reaction proceeds to completion rather than coming to equilibrium.
questions.stimulus:
The relationship between the equilibrium constant, Keq, and ΔG ° for any reaction is shown in the graph, for a limited range of ΔG ° values. The ΔH ° and TΔS ° values for the reaction between copper(I) sulfide and oxygen are provided.
[Figure: Graph of equilibrium constant Keq against ΔG° (−35 to 0 kJ mol⁻¹), with Keq very large at the most negative ΔG°; below it, the reaction equation and ΔH° = −217 kJ mol⁻¹, TΔS° = −3 kJ mol⁻¹.]

criteria.text: Provides an explanation of why the reaction proceeds to completion with reference to the data provided
Demonstrates some understanding of why the reaction proceeds to completion with reference to some of the data provided
Provides some relevant information

questions.sampleAnswer: The graph shows that reactions with large negative ΔG ° values will have extremely large equilibrium constants, ie they effectively proceed to completion. For this reaction, ΔG ° = ΔH ° - TΔS ° = -217 kJ mol⁻¹ - (-3 kJ mol⁻¹) = -214 kJ mol⁻¹ This ΔG ° value is large and negative, which means that the reaction will effectively proceed to completion. Accordingly, this reaction proceeds to completion mostly due to its large, negative ΔH ° value; the TΔS ° term is small and has little effect.

figure.alt: Graph of equilibrium constant Keq against ΔG° (−35 to 0 kJ mol⁻¹), with Keq very large at the most negative ΔG°; below it, the reaction equation and ΔH° = −217 kJ mol⁻¹, TΔS° = −3 kJ mol⁻¹.
